result:
I have always believed that the most important conversations happen not in boardrooms or at dining tables, but in the margins—those blank spaces between obligations where nothing is expected of you, where your only task is to exist in a particular patch of light and let the world continue without your commentary or consent. There is an old oak tree on the far side of the university quad where I go sometimes, not to study, not to meet anyone, not even to think in any organized way. I go simply to sit on the gnarled bench beneath it and to watch the hour change its shape. I do not bring a book, not a phone, not a notebook in which to record insights for later. I bring only the willingness to be bored, and in that boredom, to discover something older than productivity.

This is the lost art of loitering. Not the suspicious kind, not the vagrant kind that authorities frown upon, but the deliberate, leisurely kind—the kind you practiced as a child when you would wander the neighborhood with pockets full of stones and no destination, when summer afternoons stretched like warm taffy and the very idea of “making the most of your time” would have seemed as absurd as counting your heartbeats. Loitering is not laziness, though the culture that worships efficiency has tried very hard to convince us that it is. It is, rather, a different mode of attention. It is the refusal to submit every second to a purpose. When you loiter, you allow the world to happen to you without demanding that it produce a result.

I remember, with a clarity that feels almost ancestral, the summers of my childhood when my parents would disappear into their own adult worlds and leave me with the long, green afternoons to fill however I wished. I would build forts from cardboard boxes and the fallen branches of a maple tree. I would lie in the grass and watch the clouds perform their slow, continuous metamorphosis, and I would feel something that adulthood has tried to erase: the profound, restorative pleasure of being utterly unimportant to anything that needed to happen that day. There were no notifications then. There was no expectation that I should be “upskilling” or “networking” or “optimizing my mental health” through a carefully curated routine of mindfulness apps. There was only the grass, the wind, and the patient, unfolding business of being alive.

Now, of course, the architecture of our lives has changed. We live in a culture of perpetual urgency, where every idle moment is an enemy to be vanquished by content, by tasks, by the endless scroll of other people’s curated lives. We have become so afraid of emptiness that we have filled every gap—every commute, every waiting room, every brief pause between conversations—with the small, glowing rectangles that promise us entertainment, information, or the illusion of connection. I am as guilty of this as anyone. I catch myself, in the middle of a walk, reaching for my phone not because I need it, but because I have forgotten what else to do with a hand that is not holding a phone. We have trained our brains to interpret stillness as malfunction.

But stillness is not malfunction. It is the soil from which real thought grows. The neuroscientists will tell you that the brain’s default mode network—those regions that activate when we are not focused on the outside world—are responsible for some of our most essential cognitive processes: imagination, memory consolidation, self-reflection, the ability to form narratives about who we are. In other words, the brain needs its empty moments as desperately as a field needs fallow seasons. We are not designed for continuous production. We are designed for rhythms of engagement and withdrawal, and when we deny ourselves the withdrawal, we impoverish not just our rest, but our creative capacity.

There is a particular quality of awareness that arrives only when you have stopped trying to achieve something with your attention. The other afternoon, I sat on the bench beneath the oak for perhaps forty minutes—an almost scandalously long duration by modern standards—and I noticed things I would never have noticed otherwise. I noticed the way the bark of the tree was not uniform brown but a mosaic of silver, moss, and the deep rust of old wood exposed to rain. I noticed a family of ants navigating a crack in the pavement with a seriousness that rivaled any boardroom strategy session, each one carrying a fragment of leaf like a briefcase containing the meaning of existence. I noticed the light shifting in a manner so gradual that it seemed almost imperceptible, until suddenly the shadow of the bench had moved several inches, and I realized that time had passed not as a series of ticking obligations but as a slow, luminous river.

A young woman sat down on the other end of the bench, not because she knew I was having some kind of philosophical experience, but because she needed to rest her legs after walking too far in shoes that were too fashionable to be comfortable. We did not speak at first. Then she sighed loudly and said, “I just needed to not be going anywhere for a minute.” I told her I understood completely. She asked if I was waiting for someone. I said no, I was just waiting. She seemed perplexed by this, which is its own form of sad confirmation. We sat in a comfortable silence for a while, and then she told me she was a graphic designer who had spent the morning answering emails that could have been summarized in one sentence, and that she had come to this particular bench because she had seen it years ago and remembered that it was the only place where she could feel her own breath.

We exchanged a few more sentences about the weather, about the difficulty of saying “no” to tasks, about the strange sensation of being in a public space without needing to perform anything for it. Then she stood up, straightened her coat, and walked away with her phone already back in her hand, already returning to the current of urgency. But I think the moment lingered. I think she carried it with her, even if only as a faint aftertaste, a remembered permission.

There is, I believe, a politics to this kind of presence. To loiter is to resist the logic of capitalism that insists every moment of our lives must be productive, must be monetizable, must contribute to some form of self-improvement or economic value. To sit on a bench and do nothing is to insist that you are not merely a machine for work, not a node in an algorithm of efficiency, but a creature who requires unstructured time the way a garden requires rain that is not scheduled. The philosopher Bertrand Russell wrote that “the notion that work is virtuous has done immeasurable harm,” and he was right. We have made idleness into a sin, and in doing so, we have made ourselves sick.

But I do not want to romanticize this to the point of pretension. Loitering is not always comfortable. There is a vulnerability to it, especially for women, for people of color, for anyone whose presence in public space is already policed by suspicion. The right to do nothing—to exist without purpose—is not equally distributed. To advocate for loitering is also to advocate for the democratization of space, for benches that are not designed to be uncomfortable, for cities that do not criminalize rest, for a culture that does not demand constant explanation for your existence.

Still, within the spaces where I can practice it, I try to defend it. I try to treat my unstructured time as seriously as I treat my appointments, because I have come to understand that the unstructured time is where the life actually lives. It is where I remember that I am part of a continuum of consciousness that stretches back through the oak tree, through the ants, through the child on the grass years ago. It is where I remember that I do not need to earn my rest, that I do not need to justify my sitting.

If you find yourself reading this, you might be feeling that familiar itch—the one that says you should be doing something else, something more valuable, something that will show up in your resume or your bank account or your carefully curated social media presence. I want to invite you to ignore that itch, at least for a moment. Close the screen if you can. Go outside, or go to a room with a window, or simply sit where you are and allow yourself to be bored. Do not meditate with purpose; do not seek insight; do not turn your rest into another task to be optimized. Just sit. Let your mind wander like a dog that has been let off its leash, sniffing the air, following no command. You may find nothing. You may find only the feeling of your own breathing, the texture of the air against your skin, the slow revelation that the world does not require you to save it right now, and that this is a profound, almost rebellious relief.

The oak tree is still there, I imagine, growing its slow, unproductively magnificent rings, adding years to itself without checking a calendar or measuring its progress. I will go back to it when I can, not because I have a plan, but because I need to remember how to be a creature who exists in time rather than merely racing through it. The bench is waiting. The light is shifting. Nothing is required of you except to arrive. And when you arrive without purpose, you may discover that you have arrived somewhere very important indeed.

We live in a culture of perpetual urgency, where every idle moment is an enemy to be vanquished by content, by tasks, by the endless scroll of other people’s curated lives. We have become so afraid of emptiness that we have filled every gap—every commute, every waiting room, every brief pause between conversations—with the small, glowing rectangles that promise us entertainment, information, or the illusion of connection. I am as guilty of this as anyone. I catch myself, in the middle of a walk, reaching for my phone not because I need it, but because I have forgotten what else to do with a hand that is not holding a phone. We have trained our brains to interpret stillness as malfunction.

But stillness is not malfunction. It is the soil from which real thought grows. The neuroscientists will tell you that the brain’s default mode network—those regions that activate when we are not focused on the outside world—are responsible for some of our most essential cognitive processes: imagination, memory consolidation, self-reflection, the ability to form narratives about who we are. In other words, the brain needs its empty moments as desperately as a field needs fallow seasons. We are not designed for continuous production. We are designed for rhythms of engagement and withdrawal, and when we deny ourselves the withdrawal, we impoverish not just our rest, but our creative capacity.

There is a particular quality of awareness that arrives only when you have stopped trying to achieve something with your attention. The other afternoon, I sat on the bench beneath the oak for perhaps forty minutes—an almost scandalously long duration by modern standards—and I noticed things I would never have noticed otherwise. I noticed the way the bark of the tree was not uniform brown but a mosaic of silver, moss, and the deep rust of old wood exposed to rain. I noticed a family of ants navigating a crack in the pavement with a seriousness that rivaled any boardroom strategy session, each one carrying a fragment of leaf like a briefcase containing the meaning of existence. I noticed the light shifting in a manner so gradual that it seemed almost imperceptible, until suddenly the shadow of the bench had moved several inches, and I realized that time had passed not as a series of ticking obligations but as a slow, luminous river.

A young woman sat down on the other end of the bench, not because she knew I was having some kind of philosophical experience, but because she needed to rest her legs after walking too far in shoes that were too fashionable to be comfortable. We did not speak at first. Then she sighs loudly and said, “I just needed to not be going anywhere for a minute.” I told her I understood completely. She asked if I was waiting for someone. I said no, I was just waiting. She seemed perplexed by this, which is its own form of sad confirmation. We sat in a comfortable silence for a while, and then she told me she was a graphic designer who had spent the morning answering emails that could have been summarized in one sentence, and that she had come to this particular bench because she had seen it years ago and remembered that it was the only place where she could feel her own breath.

We exchanged a few more sentences about the weather, about the difficulty of saying “no” to tasks, about the strange sensation of being in a public space without needing to perform anything for it. Then she stood up, straightened her coat, and walked away with her phone already back in her hand, already returning to the current of urgency. But I think the moment lingered. I think she carried it with her, even if only as a faint aftertaste, a remembered permission.

There is, I believe, a politics to this kind of presence. To loiter is to resist the logic of capitalism that insists every moment of our lives must be productive, must be monetizable, must contribute to some form of self-improvement or economic value. To sit on a bench and do nothing is to insist that you are not merely a machine for work, not a node in an algorithm of efficiency, but a creature who requires unstructured time the way a garden requires rain that is not scheduled. The philosopher Bertrand Russell wrote that “the notion that work is virtuous has done immeasurable harm,” and he was right. We have made idleness into a sin, and in doing so, we have made ourselves sick.

But I do not want to romanticize this to the point of pretension. Loitering is not always comfortable. There is a vulnerability to it, especially for women, for people of color, for anyone whose presence in public space is already policed by suspicion. The right to do nothing—to exist without purpose—is not equally distributed. To advocate for loitering is also to advocate for the democratization of space, for benches that are not designed to be uncomfortable, for cities that do not criminalize rest, for a culture that does not demand constant explanation for your existence.

Still, within the spaces where I can practice it, I try to defend it. I try to treat my unstructured time as seriously as I treat my appointments, because I have come to understand that the unstructured time is where the life actually lives. It is where I remember that I am part of a continuum of consciousness that stretches back through the oak tree, through the ants, through the child on the grass years ago. It is where I remember that I do not need to earn my rest, that I do not need to justify my sitting.

If you find yourself reading this, you might be feeling that familiar itch—the one that says you should be doing something else, something more valuable, something that will show up in your resume or your bank account or your carefully curated social media presence. I want to invite you to ignore that itch, at least for a moment. Close the screen if you can. Go outside, or go to a room with a window, or simply sit where you are and allow yourself to be bored. Do not meditate with purpose; do not seek insight; do not turn your rest into another task to be optimized. Just sit. Let your mind wander like a dog that has been let off its leash, sniffing the air, following no command. You may find nothing. You may find only the feeling of your own breathing, the texture of the air against your skin, the slow revelation that the world does not require you to save it right now, and that this is a profound, almost rebellious relief.

The oak tree is still there, I imagine, growing its slow, unproductively magnificent rings, adding years to itself without checking a calendar or measuring its progress. I will go back to it when I can, not because I have a plan, but because I need to remember how to be a creature who exists in time rather than merely racing through it. The bench is waiting. The light is shifting. Nothing is required of you except to arrive. And when you arrive without purpose, you may discover that you have arrived somewhere very important indeed.
